# Charter

## Use cases

### Durable engineering processes

Humans and agents working in engineering use grimore to build durable
engineering processes without coaxing agents into operating effectively -
across code development, process optimization, and design. The project
exists so that alignment between humans and agents produces better tools.

## Constraints

### Cross-platform across agent consumers

grimore must work with different agents as consumers. It cannot be a tool
that only works in Claude Code, or Codex, or any single harness -
cross-platform support across agent consumers is a standing requirement of
the project, not a later portability effort.

## Non-goals

### Bug-finding and review judgments

explain-diff explains intent and implications; it does not judge code or hunt
for bugs. A guide says what changed, why, which decisions are load-bearing and
what remains open - it never reports a defect or rates quality. Excluded
because mixing the two changes how the output is read: a document that
sometimes judges invites the reader to treat silence as approval, and code
review is a separate job with a separate standard of evidence.

### Hosted publishing of change guides

explain-diff writes a self-contained local HTML file and does not publish it
to any hosted surface; hosted publishing may be added later as an option, but
local HTML stays canonical. Excluded because a self-contained file needs no
account, no network, and no retention policy - and a change guide routinely
embeds code that has not been reviewed for disclosure.

### Multi-diff comparisons, timelines, and PDF

explain-diff explains one diff. Comparing several diffs side by side,
rendering history timelines across a series of changes, and PDF generation
beyond what the print stylesheet already produces are all excluded. Excluded
as YAGNI: each is a distinct product with its own navigation and state, and
the print CSS already covers the one export anyone actually asked for.

### Automatic external-store pointer writes

finish-docs does not write pointer or status records into external knowledge
and tracking stores automatically; keeping such a store in sync remains a
session-level habit. Excluded because automatic writes would couple the
reconciliation pass to a specific external tool that not every adopting
project has, and that coupling is hard to undo once workflows depend on it.
Revisit after v1, once the manual habit has shown what is actually worth
writing.

### Full staleness tripwire

Coverage reporting, path-hygiene tooling that detects stale or renamed
`paths:` globs, and any semantic comparison of a diff against doc content are
out of scope for v1. The minimal touched-path guard ships instead, and is
deliberately crude: it cannot report what fraction of the codebase is
documented, cannot notice when a declared glob stops matching anything, and
cannot tell a meaningful change from a trivial one. Deferred because each
addition needs either a semantic model of the diff or a maintenance surface of
its own, and neither earns its cost before the basic guard has been lived
with.

### Multi-context glossaries

One glossary per repository. The CONTEXT-MAP pattern, where a word carries
different definitions in different bounded contexts, is excluded from v1: it
would require every term to declare a context, every consumer to know which
context it reads in, and the Avoid-term lint to become context-aware. Excluded
because a repository whose glossary genuinely needs two conflicting
definitions of one word has a naming problem the glossary should force it to
resolve, not a tooling gap.

### A rejected component status

Components have three statuses - draft, current, superseded - and no fourth
for options considered and turned down. A rejected alternative is recorded
inside the body of the component that records the decision actually taken,
where a reader meets it alongside the reasoning, rather than as a separate
component that renders nowhere and accumulates in the store. Excluded because
a status that never appears in any consumer output is bookkeeping, not
documentation.

### Semantic drift detection beyond supersede edges

Status banners on specs and plans track explicit supersede edges only. A
decision reversed by a fresh component carrying no `supersedes:` edge fires no
banner, and grimore does not try to infer such reversals by comparing
component content. Excluded because that inference is a semantic judgment that
would be either unreliable or expensive, and edge-writing at branch finish is
a reviewed step precisely so the graph stays honest rather than guessed.

### Static-site generator integration

grim emits static-site-ready markdown and stops there. Integration with a
particular generator - theme wiring, navigation config, build hooks,
deployment - is excluded. Excluded because every generator wants its own
frontmatter and directory conventions, so adopting one would either force that
choice on every project or grow a plugin surface per generator; emitting clean
markdown lets a project wire up whatever it already uses.
